titulo: Linking Words — Part 1: Contrast and Concession
descricao: The words that show contrast and concession — whereas, while, although, even though, despite, however, nevertheless, and more. Learn which grammatical structure each one requires and how to stop confusing them.

secoes.titulo: What Are Linking Words — and Why Do They Matter?
secoes.conteudo:
When you connect two ideas in English, the word you choose to connect them does more than hold the sentence together. It signals the relationship between those ideas — whether the second idea adds to the first, contradicts it, explains it, or limits it. These connecting words are called **linking words**, though you will also hear them called **connectors**, **discourse markers**, or **transition words**. All four terms refer to the same thing: words and phrases that show how ideas relate to each other.

Native speakers use linking words constantly — in conversation, in writing, in any situation where ideas need to be organized and communicated clearly. At B1-B2 level, the absence of linking words is one of the clearest signals of a learner who has not yet reached fluency. The sentences may all be grammatically correct, but they sit next to each other without connection, without logical flow, without the tissue that makes language feel natural.

This material covers the most essential and most confused group: the words that express **contrast** and **concession**. Contrast says: 'these two things are different.' Concession says: 'I admit X is true, but Y is still the case.' Both involve a tension between two ideas — and English has a rich vocabulary for expressing that tension in different ways, with different grammatical structures. Understanding which structure each word requires is the key that unlocks the whole system.

secoes.titulo: Direct Contrast — Whereas, While, Unlike, On the Other Hand
secoes.conteudo:
When two things or situations are simply different, English has four main tools for saying so cleanly and precisely.

**Whereas** is the most elegant contrast word in English. It places two opposite facts side by side and says: look at the difference. 'Brazil has a warm climate, **whereas** England is often cold and grey.' 'She prefers to work in the morning, **whereas** her partner does his best work at night.' **Whereas** belongs mostly to written and formal English — it signals careful, structured thinking. In everyday conversation, 'but' usually takes its place.

**While** shares this contrast function — and this is where learners must be careful. **While** has two completely different jobs in English. When it refers to time, it means 'during the time that': 'She called me **while** I was cooking.' When it expresses contrast, it means exactly the same as **whereas**: 'She loves cities, **while** her brother prefers the countryside.' The meaning is always clear from context, but you need to be aware that the same word is doing two different jobs.

**Unlike** introduces a contrast using a noun, not a clause. 'Unlike his sister, Marco is very quiet.' 'Unlike many cities, this one has excellent public transport.' The structure is fixed: **unlike** + noun phrase + comma + the contrasting fact. You cannot say 'unlike she is quiet' — **unlike** requires a noun, not a verb clause.

**On the other hand** introduces the second side of a comparison after you have established the first. 'Living in a city offers endless opportunities. **On the other hand**, it can be expensive and noisy.' It signals that you are about to see the other angle. Notice that it does not go inside a single sentence — it begins a new sentence or clause after a pause. **By contrast** and **in contrast** work similarly: 'The north of the country is mountainous. **By contrast**, the south is flat and warm.'

Concession is slightly more complex than direct contrast — and more powerful. A concession says: 'I acknowledge this fact, and yet it does not change my conclusion.' The two ideas are in tension, and the concession connector holds that tension in a single sentence.

**Although** is the standard concession conjunction. 'Although it was raining, we decided to go for a walk.' 'She passed the exam, although she hadn't studied much.' The structure is flexible: **although** can open the sentence (introducing the concession first) or come in the middle (introducing it after the main fact). Both are natural and both are correct. What changes is the emphasis: starting with **although** gives more weight to the concession; ending with it puts the main point first.

**Even though** is stronger than **although**. It adds an emotional layer — a sense of 'despite all of that, despite what you might expect.' 'She kept smiling, **even though** she was exhausted.' 'He passed, **even though** the exam was extremely difficult.' Use **even though** when you want to signal that the contrast is particularly striking or surprising. In everyday speech, **even though** is more common than **although** because it carries more feeling.

**Though** is the informal version of **although**. It works in all the same grammatical positions but sounds more casual: 'Though it was early, the café was already busy.' And it has one extra trick: **though** can go at the very end of a sentence as a standalone comment. 'She's good at her job. She's not very friendly, **though**.' That final position — a comma and 'though' — is entirely natural in spoken English and in informal writing. **Although** and **even though** cannot do this.

secoes.titulo: Concession with a Noun — Despite, In Spite Of
secoes.conteudo:
**Despite** and **in spite of** express exactly the same idea as **although** and **even though** — but with a completely different grammatical structure. This is where many learners make the most consistent linking word error.

**Despite** and **in spite of** are prepositions. They do not connect two clauses — they connect a main clause to a noun or a gerund (the -ing form of a verb). 'Despite the rain, we went for a walk.' 'In spite of the difficulty, she kept going.' 'Despite feeling tired, he finished the presentation.'

The classic error: 'Despite she was tired, she finished.' This is wrong — **despite** cannot be followed by a subject and a verb. For that structure, you need **although**: 'Although she was tired, she finished.' If you want to use **despite**, you must convert the clause to a noun or gerund: 'Despite her tiredness, she finished.' / 'Despite being tired, she finished.'

One structure that bridges the gap: **despite the fact that** + clause. 'Despite the fact that she was tired, she finished.' This allows **despite** to precede a full clause — but by wrapping the clause inside a noun phrase with 'the fact that.' It is slightly long and formal, so in most situations, **although** is the simpler and more natural choice.

**Despite** and **in spite of** mean exactly the same thing. **In spite of** is slightly less formal and slightly more common in spoken English. There is no meaningful difference in meaning — choose whichever sounds better in context. What never changes is the rule: both must be followed by a noun or gerund, never a subject-verb clause.

secoes.titulo: Result of Concession — However, Nevertheless, Nonetheless, Yet, Still
secoes.conteudo:
This group does something slightly different from the words above. Rather than joining two parts of one sentence, they connect two separate sentences — acknowledging the first sentence and then turning in a different direction. They say: 'I have just told you X. Now here is the complicating fact.'

**However** is the most common and versatile of these words. It works in writing and in conversation. 'She trained every day. **However**, she didn't make the team.' 'The plan sounds good. **However**, there are a few problems we need to discuss.' **However** always comes after a complete sentence — either at the start of the next sentence or after a semicolon. The critical grammar point: **however** must be separated from the rest of the sentence by a comma. 'However, she didn't make the team.' The comma is not optional.

**Nevertheless** and **nonetheless** are more formal synonyms of **however**. They are common in academic writing, formal reports, and careful prose. They carry a slightly stronger sense of 'despite all of that': 'The evidence is unclear. **Nevertheless**, a decision must be made.' Both words are interchangeable in meaning — **nevertheless** is slightly more common in British English, **nonetheless** slightly more common in American English, but the difference is minimal.

**Yet** as a linking word belongs mostly to writing. 'She had everything she needed. **Yet** something felt missing.' It creates a sense of literary tension — the turn is unexpected, and **yet** signals that expectation is about to be overturned. In speech, 'but' takes its place.

**Still** in this function means 'despite what was just said, this remains true.' 'He apologized. **Still**, she found it hard to forgive him.' It is used informally, mostly in speech. The emphasis is on persistence — the second fact holds despite the first.

secoes.titulo: Grammar Focus — Three Structures, One Idea
secoes.conteudo:
The most important grammar insight in this material is this: the same meaning — 'idea X, but idea Y' — can be expressed through three completely different grammatical structures. Understanding which structure each word requires is the key to using linking words correctly.

**Conjunctions** join two clauses inside a single sentence. The words in this group: **although**, **even though**, **though**, **whereas**, **while** (contrast). Structure: conjunction + clause, + main clause. Or: main clause + conjunction + clause. 'Although it was raining, we went out.' / 'We went out, although it was raining.' Both are correct — the order changes the emphasis.

Prepositions are followed by a noun or gerund, not a clause. The words: **despite**, **in spite of**, **unlike**. Structure: preposition + noun or gerund phrase + comma + main clause. 'Despite the rain, we went out.' / 'Despite raining heavily, we went out.' There is no subject-verb clause after the preposition.

**Conjunctive adverbs** connect two separate sentences. The words: **however**, **nevertheless**, **nonetheless**, **yet**, **still**, **on the other hand**, **by contrast**. Structure: Sentence 1. Conjunctive adverb + comma + Sentence 2. 'It was raining. However, we went out.' Alternative: Sentence 1; conjunctive adverb + comma + Sentence 2. 'It was raining; however, we went out.'

The classic error is mixing categories: 'Despite she studied hard, she failed.' (preposition followed by a clause) or 'Although the rain, we went out.' (conjunction followed by a noun). Identify which category your word belongs to — then build the correct structure around it.

**However** versus **although**. These two words carry similar meaning, but they are not interchangeable grammatically. **Although** is a conjunction and joins clauses inside one sentence: 'Although she was tired, she continued.' **However** is a **conjunctive adverb** and connects two separate sentences: 'She was tired. However, she continued.' Putting **however** in the middle of a single clause with just a comma is a **comma splice** — a well-known grammar error in formal writing: 'She was tired, however she continued.' ✗ The fix is a semicolon ('She was tired; however, she continued') or a full stop followed by a new sentence.

**Despite** versus **although**. Both express concession, but they require different grammar. **Despite** needs a noun or gerund: 'Despite the cold.' **Although** needs a subject + verb: 'Although it was cold.' Mixing them — 'Despite it was cold' — is one of the most frequent errors at B1 level. Convert the clause to a noun: 'Despite the cold weather' or 'Despite it being cold.'

**While** — time or contrast? In most sentences the meaning is obvious: 'While she slept' (time) versus 'While he is quiet, she never stops talking' (contrast). But some sentences are genuinely ambiguous. When contrast is your intended meaning and the sentence might be misread as a time reference, use **whereas** instead — it can only ever mean contrast.

**On the contrary** versus **on the other hand**. These are often confused, but they do different jobs. **On the other hand** introduces the second side of a genuine two-sided comparison, where both sides are valid: 'Living in a city is exciting. On the other hand, it is expensive.' **On the contrary** is a correction — it pushes back against what was just said: 'You look tired.' 'On the contrary, I feel great.' It means 'the opposite is true,' not 'here is another angle.' Using **on the contrary** where you mean **on the other hand** makes your response sound like a contradiction rather than a balanced observation.
